ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Seattle, WA
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging and UT weld inspection for Seattle hulls, ferry terminals, refineries and port steel, mobilized to your site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Gauging in Seattle, Washington
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes ultrasonic testing technicians to Seattle and Puget Sound sites for hull and tank plate gauging, pipe and vessel wall surveys, and shear-wave examination of welds. If your asset sits on a pier, in a dry dock, in a refinery or on a waterfront crane, send us the drawings and the code and we will build the scope around the access you actually have. Request a UT quote for your Seattle job and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Seattle

Seattle's steel lives on the water. The Sound carries a working fleet of ferries, tugs, fishing vessels, cargo ships and Navy hulls, and every one of them loses plate to corrosion that only a thickness survey measures. The dry docks on Harbor Island and across the water at Bremerton, and the Washington State Ferries maintenance yard at Eagle Harbor on Bainbridge Island, are where hull plating, ballast tanks, shaft tubes and rudder stock are gauged against original scantlings and class or Navy allowances. Container terminals along Elliott Bay and the Duwamish Waterway add gantry cranes, rails and bollard foundations in salt air.

Inland from the shore the same method serves land-based plants. Western Washington has refineries at Cherry Point, Ferndale, Anacortes and Tacoma, so piping, columns and tanks need wall-loss tracking. State ferry terminals carry steel piling, transfer spans, overhead loading structures and dolphins that are painted, inspected and repaired on a rolling schedule. Utilities such as Seattle City Light operate dams and steel penstocks in the Cascades that are surveyed during unit outages, and fabrication shops across the region need plate and weld checks before steel is shipped.

  • Ship and ferry hull plating, ballast and fuel tanks, shaft and rudder stock: thickness gauging at docking
  • Terminal and pier steel: piling, transfer spans, trestle members, crane runways
  • Refinery and industrial piping, vessels and tank floors: wall thickness at fixed locations
  • Penstocks and water-conveyance steel: wall-loss surveys during outages

What ultrasonic testing finds and what it misses

An ultrasonic instrument launches a short pulse into steel and reads the time it takes to return. On a thickness job the echo comes from the opposite face, so the readout is remaining wall. On a weld job the echo comes from planar and volumetric flaws inside the joint, the sort that cannot be seen from the surface: lack of fusion, cracks, slag and porosity. That is why UT is the method used to answer how much steel is left and whether a repair weld is sound.

Marine and waterfront steel pushes the method hard. Heavy marine growth, scale and coatings have to be removed from the reading area before the probe sits flat. Pitted plate gives scattered echoes, so a trained eye on the A-scan matters more than the number on the screen. Rough corroded surfaces and curved shell plate can make probe contact poor, and a single reading says nothing about the plate three inches away, so the grid spacing is chosen to find localized loss and not just average it out. Cracks that break the surface of ferromagnetic steel are usually found faster by magnetic particle testing, and for aluminum or stainless the surface method is penetrant testing; we point you to those when they fit better.

Codes, class rules and Washington requirements

The technique follows ASME Section V Article 4 for weld examination and Article 5 for materials, with ASTM E797 for contact thickness measurement. Acceptance comes from the code that governs the asset. Process piping and vessels refer to ASME B31.3 and ASME Section VIII, structural steel to AWS D1.1, and in-service refinery equipment is tracked under API 510, API 570 and API 653 with the owner's authorized inspector responsible for the inspection. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work and hands that inspector the data. Ship hulls are surveyed to the requirements of the vessel's classification society or, for Navy work, the contract specification, and class-credited thickness measurement has its own approval rules that the owner or surveyor sets; we confirm exactly what your surveyor will accept before accepting a hull scope.

Washington regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Department of Labor and Industries, which administers chapter 296-104 of the Washington Administrative Code under chapter 70.79 RCW. Special inspectors hold a Washington commission, and owner-user inspection agencies with an established inspection department can inspect their own equipment to a nationally recognized standard. Equipment needs a certificate of inspection, so the thickness data we report often becomes part of the case an owner presents for the interval it selects. Our explainer on thickness measurement requirements covers the Section V rules. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) adds a duty for process plants to inspect to good engineering practice. State ferry terminal work follows WSDOT inspection practice, described on the ferry terminal maintenance page.

Gauging technique on corroded and coated steel

For corroded hull plate and pipe, technicians use a dual-element probe, which keeps the transmitter and receiver separate and handles pitted back walls better than a single crystal. The setup is calibrated on a step block cut from the same grade of steel as the work, the zero and velocity are checked, and the check is repeated at the end of the session. Reading the A-scan trace lets the technician reject a doubled echo on thin plate and notice a lamination reflecting from mid-wall. Coating thickness can be accounted for by an echo-to-echo mode on instruments that support it; where we use that mode, it is verified on a coated sample first.

Readings are recorded on a plan that matches the hull or the isometric: frame spacing and plate strakes for a ship, condition monitoring locations for a pipe. Hot lines need a high-temperature probe, a couplant rated for it and a temperature correction. Overhead and confined spaces, common inside ballast tanks, require rescue and ventilation plans that the vessel owner supplies and that must be agreed before entry.

Weld examination with shear waves

For welds the technician scans with an angle-beam probe, often 45, 60 or 70 degrees, from both sides of the joint where geometry allows. A reference level is set from side-drilled holes in a block of matching thickness, and indications above the evaluation level are located, measured and compared with the acceptance rule. Lack of fusion and cracks in a bevel weld reflect best at the matching angle, so the scan plan names the angles chosen for each joint. On a ship repair, structural weld or terminal steel detail, the written procedure is approved by an ASNT Level III before the job and is the reference the surveyor or engineer reads the result against.

Who performs the work

Atlantis technicians work under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician calibrates the equipment, performs the examination and interprets results, while an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews the reports; our Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis has no office in Seattle. Technicians travel to your site, yard or vessel for the agreed scope, and we confirm travel, safe-entry and orientation requirements at the quote stage. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If a class society, the Navy or a prime contractor requires a specific qualification, say so at the start.

Typical UT findings on marine and terminal steel

On hull plate the common finding is general wastage on the bottom and splash zone, with deeper localized pitting beside weld seams and under old coating damage. Ballast tanks show grooving along stiffener welds and heavy loss on tank-top plating. Terminal piling and transfer span members lose steel fastest at the splash zone and at bolted or welded joints where water sits. On refinery piping the finds are localized loss at elbows and dead legs. Each result is reported against the nominal and minimum allowable values you supply, and the readings closest to the limit are flagged so the surveyor or owner can decide whether to renew steel, coat and monitor, or reinspect at the next docking. The technician reports what was measured and leaves renewal decisions to the owner and surveyor.

What the UT report contains

A complete report records the component or hull location, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block, the couplant and surface condition, the technician and level, and the ambient and surface temperature when it matters. Thickness reports include the full reading grid, the nominal thickness and the allowable minimum where you provide them, and the percentage of diminution where the surveyor wants it. Weld reports include a sketch of each indication with position, length and amplitude against the reference level and an accept or reject call against the named criteria. A Level III reviews the report before release. Tell us the layout your surveyor or inspector wants.

Planning a UT job in Seattle

Puget Sound weather and logistics decide most jobs. Winters are wet and cool, and steel that is wet will not take couplant cleanly or hold a probe still, so enclosures and drying plans are normal. Waterfront steel is salty and often coated, which means surface prep time. Dry-dock slots are booked far ahead and are short, so hull gauging must be scheduled to the docking plan and the access staging, not squeezed in. Ferry terminal work depends on tides and vessel schedules, and work from a barge adds weather windows. Refineries in Whatcom and Skagit counties and in Tacoma run badge and safety orientation steps that take time. Tell us about those constraints early, because the right plan on paper saves the dock day.

UT, MT or PT for your Seattle job

Use UT for remaining wall and internal weld flaws. Use magnetic particle testing in Seattle for surface cracks in carbon steel such as crane pedestals, hatch corners and repair welds. Use penetrant testing in Seattle for aluminum, stainless and other non-magnetic work on vessels and in plants. Many shipyard and terminal scopes need two or all three. Our national ultrasonic testing page and the ultrasonic testing guide explain the service and the physics in general terms.

Training your own UT technicians

A shipyard or plant that gauges every year may prefer its own qualified technicians. Atlantis teaches UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 through online theory and a practical examination at your facility, and your written practice defines who is qualified under SNT-TC-1A. Trainees can build scanning skill on the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator. Seattle employers can read about NDT training in Seattle, check SNT-TC-1A eligibility or try the practice tests. Statewide coverage is on the Washington inspection services page.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Seattle?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Seattle. Technicians travel to your vessel, yard, terminal or plant for the agreed scope, and we confirm travel, safe-entry and orientation requirements in the quote.

faq.q: Can you gauge hull plate in a dry dock?
faq.a: Yes, by mobilizing technicians to the dock for the booked window. The scope follows your gauging plan and the surveyor requirements, and we confirm in advance what data and format your surveyor will accept.

faq.q: Is your thickness data accepted for class surveys?
faq.a: Class-credited thickness measurement has its own approval rules set by the classification society and the surveyor. Atlantis confirms what your surveyor will accept before accepting a hull scope, so the readings are used the way you intend.

faq.q: Which codes do you use for UT?
faq.a: ASME Section V Articles 4 and 5 and ASTM E797 for technique, with acceptance from the code governing the asset, such as ASME B31.3, Section VIII, AWS D1.1 or the vessel specification. The owner names the code before work starts.

faq.q: Do you act as the API inspector on refinery work?
faq.a: No. On refinery equipment the authorized inspector for the owner remains responsible under API 510, 570 and 653. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work and gives that inspector the thickness and indication data they need.

faq.q: How do Washington boiler rules affect UT data?
faq.a: The Department of Labor and Industries administers boiler and pressure vessel law, and equipment needs a certificate of inspection. Fixed-location thickness records help the commissioned inspector or owner-user agency decide on inspection intervals.

faq.q: What surface preparation do you need?
faq.a: The reading area must be free of loose scale, marine growth and flaking coating so the probe sits flat with couplant. Heavier coatings may need an echo-to-echo method that is verified on a sample first.

faq.q: What should I send to get a quote?
faq.a: Drawings or the gauging plan, the code or class rule, material and expected thickness, coating condition, access method such as dock, staging or barge, the schedule window and any site orientation requirements.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Seattle, WA | MPI
mt.description: Mag particle testing of crane pedestals, hull weld details, bridge steel and refinery welds around Seattle and Puget Sound, mobilized to site. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Seattle, Washington
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes magnetic particle technicians to Seattle and Puget Sound sites to find surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel: crane pedestals, hatch corners, rudder and skeg attachments, bridge and pier steel, refinery weld repairs and lifting equipment. Send the component list and the code and we will plan the examination around your access. Request an MT quote for your Seattle site and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Seattle

The Seattle area builds, repairs and moves heavy steel, and most of it is exposed to fatigue and weather. Shipyards and dry docks on Harbor Island and at Bremerton handle hull repairs where the steel renewal scope depends on what a surface examination finds at fatigue-prone details: hatch coamings, crane pedestals, bulwark attachments, engine foundations and the welds around rudder horns and skegs. The ferry fleet and its terminals add vehicle ramps, transfer spans and overhead loading structures that flex with every crossing and carry cracks that begin at weld toes.

On land, western Washington's refineries bring vessels, nozzle welds and pipe supports into scope during turnarounds. The container terminals on Elliott Bay and the Duwamish Waterway rely on gantry cranes whose boom hinges, sheave pins and structural welds are examined on a maintenance cycle. Construction in the city keeps tower cranes and mobile lifting gear busy, and hooks, shackles and load-bearing welds on that equipment are examined before and after heavy jobs. Hydro and thermal plants in the region have turbine components, headers and attachment welds that take MT during outages, and fabricators across the metro build structural steel where in-process weld checks catch defects early.

  • Hull and deck details: coamings, pedestals, attachments, foundations, repair welds
  • Ferry and terminal steel: vehicle ramps, transfer span members, loading structure welds
  • Port and construction cranes: hooks, pins, boom welds, lifting lugs
  • Refinery and plant steel: nozzle, support and attachment welds, repaired areas

What MT detects and what it cannot

Magnetic particle testing works on ferromagnetic steel only. The part is magnetized, fine particles are applied, and any crack or seam that breaks or sits just below the surface leaks magnetic flux and holds a visible line of particles. It finds fatigue cracks, crater cracks, lack of fusion at the surface and laps on carbon and low-alloy steel. It cannot be used on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or bronze, which are common on vessels in this region, and it will not find flaws deep inside a weld.

Two practical limits matter on Puget Sound steel. Sensitivity falls when the surface is rough, scaled or covered by thick paint or marine growth, so prep has to be agreed in advance. And because a crack shows best when it crosses the field, the code requires the examination to be repeated with the field turned about ninety degrees. A single pass is not an examination. For aluminum and stainless, use penetrant testing; for wall thickness and internal flaws, use ultrasonic testing.

Codes, class rules and Washington requirements

The technique is set by ASME Section V Article 7, with ASTM E709 as a guide and ASTM E1444 as the practice. Acceptance depends on the asset. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 covers pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 covers process piping, AWS D1.1 covers structural steel, and AWS D1.5 applies to bridge steel when a state agency is the owner. Hull and Navy work are surveyed to the classification society rules or the contract specification, and we confirm which one applies before agreeing to a scope.

Washington's boiler and pressure vessel law is administered by the Department of Labor and Industries and the Board of Boiler Rules, using the National Board Inspection Code for repairs. A repair or alteration on registered equipment needs a repair organization that holds the right authorization, and the examination records of the excavation and the finished weld are part of what the commissioned inspector reviews. The National Board describes the repair framework. For ferry terminal structure, the Washington State Department of Transportation explains its inspection and repair approach on the ferry terminal maintenance page. Process plants also carry a mechanical integrity duty under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j). For a plain-language read of the technique rules, see the Article 7 explainer.

How the examination is carried out

For field work the technician uses an electromagnetic yoke. An alternating-current yoke has to show a lifting power of at least 10 pounds at the pole spacing in use, and a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, checked with a test weight before use. The yoke is set across the weld, particles are dusted or sprayed on while the field is active, and the area is read; then the yoke is rotated roughly ninety degrees for the second pass. Prods stay off finished pressure-retaining and fatigue-critical surfaces, because arc burns create new problems.

Wet fluorescent particles are chosen for higher sensitivity, for example on fatigue-critical details or hydrogen service, and require a darkened area and a UV-A lamp whose intensity is checked. Visible dry powder suits rough outdoor welds. A field indicator confirms the setup produces a usable field. Where residual magnetism could disturb later welding, machining or sensitive instruments, the part is demagnetized and measured. Coated steel can be examined through a thin non-magnetic coating only up to the thickness the procedure demonstrates, so thicker marine paint has to be removed in the examination area first.

Surface preparation on waterfront and marine steel

Preparation decides how good an examination can be. Shipyard and pier steel arrives coated, salted and fouled, and the examination area has to be brought back to clean metal or to a coating that is thin enough for the procedure to allow. Cleaning might be wire brushing, needle scaling, light grinding or abrasive blasting, and it has to be finished before the particles go on because a dirty surface holds particles that look like indications. Oil and grease must be removed or the particles clump. Weld spatter and sharp profiles are dressed so that false indications do not mask real ones.

On ships and terminals the cleaning work often belongs to someone other than the inspection crew, so it is scheduled alongside the dry-dock or terminal work plan. When blasting or painting contractors are working nearby, the examination window has to be sequenced between them, because a freshly painted surface cannot be examined and a freshly examined surface should not be recoated until the owner has accepted the result.

Common MT findings and what happens next

On Puget Sound steel the typical finds are fatigue cracks at the toes of attachment welds, cracking at the corners of cutouts and openings, and crater cracks at weld ends. Crane and lifting equipment show cracks in hook throats and at pin bores. Many rounded or very short indications turn out to be non-relevant, from a section change or rough surface, and are re-examined after light cleaning. A confirmed linear indication is marked, measured and reported. The owner, engineer or surveyor decides whether to grind, repair, renew or monitor it, and Atlantis does not make that call. After a repair, the same examination is repeated to show the crack is gone, and both reports are filed together so the history of the detail is complete.

Photographs of the marked indication and a sketch tied to a frame number or a drawing grid let the next crew find the same detail quickly, which makes year-over-year comparisons straightforward.

Who performs the work

Technicians work under the Atlantis written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians perform the examination, set up the equipment and interpret indications; the procedure and the final reports go to an ASNT NDT Level III, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis has no office in Seattle. We mobilize crews to your yard, vessel, terminal or plant with the yokes, lamps and consumables the procedure needs, and confirm travel and orientation requirements in the quote. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If a class society or a prime contractor has a specific personnel requirement, tell us at the start.

What an MT report contains

Each report identifies the component and location, the procedure and revision, the yoke or equipment and its lift check, the particle type and carrier, the surface condition, the ultraviolet and ambient light readings for fluorescent work, and the technician and level. Indications are plotted on a sketch with position and length, and the disposition is stated against the criteria you named. Where the owner decides on grinding or repair, the same examination is repeated afterward and filed beside the original. The report is then reviewed by the same Level III before it is released to you.

Planning an MT job in Seattle

Damp weather is the main variable. Rain stops outdoor examination and wet steel will not hold particles, so enclosures, tarps and drying equipment are part of the plan, and winter temperatures near freezing slow the carrier fluid and change how particles behave. Salt and marine growth on waterfront steel require cleaning before readings. Dry-dock windows are short and booked in advance, ferry terminal work follows tides and vessel schedules, and overwater work from a barge depends on sea state. Refinery and port sites run badge and safety orientation steps that need lead time. Tell us the access reality and the schedule window early, and we will plan around them.

MT, PT or UT for your Seattle job

A scoping conversation settles most choices. Describe the material, the coating state and the fatigue or repair concern, and we will recommend the method that answers it, and whether pairing it with a second method on the same mobilization saves you a return visit to the yard.

For surface cracks in carbon steel, MT is fast and sensitive. For aluminum, stainless or bronze, such as vessel superstructure and propeller hardware, choose penetrant testing in Seattle. For wall loss and internal weld flaws, choose ultrasonic testing in Seattle. Many hull repairs combine all three. Our national magnetic particle testing page, the complete MT guide and the MT versus PT comparison cover the service and theory in general terms.

Training your own MT technicians

If you would rather have in-house capability, Atlantis offers MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and the magnetic particle testing training page explains how a course and practical fit your written practice. Seattle employers can read about NDT training in Seattle, and statewide coverage is on the Washington inspection services page. For a written practice, see written practice development.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Seattle?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Seattle. Crews are mobilized to your yard, vessel, terminal or plant with the yokes, lamps and particles the procedure needs, and travel details are confirmed in the quote.

faq.q: Can MT be used on aluminum or stainless steel?
faq.a: No. Magnetic particle testing needs ferromagnetic material. Aluminum, austenitic stainless steel and bronze do not hold a useful field, so penetrant testing is the method for surface cracks in those metals.

faq.q: Why is every area examined twice?
faq.a: A crack shows best when it crosses the magnetic field, so ASME Section V Article 7 requires a second examination with the field turned roughly ninety degrees. A single pass can miss a crack running parallel to the field.

faq.q: Can you examine through marine paint?
faq.a: A thin non-magnetic coating can stay in place only if the procedure has shown it works at that thickness. Anything heavier is removed in the examination area, or the procedure is demonstrated on a painted sample.

faq.q: What details on a ship do you examine?
faq.a: Typical scopes are hatch coamings, crane pedestals, bulwark and foundation attachments and repair welds on carbon steel, as agreed with the owner or surveyor. Aluminum and stainless parts are covered by penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: Which code sets acceptance?
faq.a: The code or rule that governs the item: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6, ASME B31.3, AWS D1.1 or D1.5, or the class or contract specification for a vessel. We confirm it before the job.

faq.q: Does Washington require anything for repair records?
faq.a: Repairs on registered boilers and pressure vessels follow the National Board Inspection Code under the Department of Labor and Industries. Magnetic particle records of the excavation and finished weld support the commissioned inspector review.

faq.q: Who reviews your MT reports?
faq.a: An ASNT NDT Level III reviews each report and approves the procedure. Level II technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, perform the examination and interpret indications.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Seattle, WA
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing of aluminum, stainless and alloy welds, shafts and castings around Seattle and Puget Sound, mobilized to your site. Ask for a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Seattle, Washington
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes liquid penetrant technicians to Seattle and Puget Sound sites to find surface-breaking cracks, pores and laps in non-magnetic metals and machined parts: aluminum vessel structure, stainless piping, propeller and shaft components, castings and alloy repairs. Request a PT quote for your Seattle job with the material, part list and code, and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Seattle

Seattle's maritime economy runs on metals that magnetic methods cannot examine. Ferries, workboats, fishing vessels and yachts built or repaired around Puget Sound often carry aluminum superstructure and stainless piping, and bronze or stainless propellers and shafts. After a weld repair, a grounding or a docking, penetrant testing is the practical way to confirm that the repaired joint has no open cracks. Naval and commercial yards use it on stainless systems and non-ferrous fittings where the contract names a surface method.

On land, the region's refineries have stainless and alloy piping, exchanger tube-to-tubesheet welds and weld overlay that need surface examination during turnarounds. The Seattle area also has a large biotechnology, food and beverage and brewing sector whose stainless tanks, skids and sanitary piping are welded and checked before they are commissioned. Machine shops and foundries produce valve bodies, housings and castings in stainless, aluminum and bronze, and penetrant is the usual screen for cracks and shrinkage openings in those parts.

  • Aluminum and stainless vessel structure, fittings and weld repairs
  • Propellers, shafts, valve bodies and bronze or stainless castings
  • Refinery stainless and alloy piping welds, overlay and tube joints
  • Stainless tanks and process piping in biotech, food and beverage plants

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

Penetrant testing finds flaws that are open to the surface and nothing else. A thin liquid soaks into cracks and pores, the surplus is wiped away, and a developer lifts the trapped liquid into a visible mark. It works on any non-porous material, magnetic or not, which is why it is the default method for aluminum, stainless and bronze. A very fine crack shows as a visible line once developer draws the liquid out.

It cannot see a flaw that is closed to the surface, no matter how serious. Smeared metal from grinding or machining can close the mouth of a real crack, and paint, oil, scale or marine growth stops the liquid entering. Rough castings and porous materials leave a heavy background that hides small indications. For internal flaws or remaining wall, ultrasonic testing is the correct method, and on carbon steel the magnetic particle method is often faster.

Codes and acceptance criteria for PT

The technique comes from ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165. Acceptance follows the governing code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural welds, or the class rule or contract specification for a vessel. Where a Navy contract names its own standard, we confirm which one applies before accepting the scope. In each case the code, not the technician, sets what counts as a rejectable indication.

Washington's Department of Labor and Industries administers boiler and pressure vessel law, so penetrant records on repaired registered equipment go to a commissioned inspector or an owner-user inspection agency. Repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code, described by the National Board. For the technique rules in plain terms, read our explainer on Article 6 requirements. Process plants also have a mechanical integrity duty under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j). Nuclear and aerospace customers sometimes name different standards altogether, and we will tell you plainly if a customer-specific requirement is beyond our written practice.

Choosing the penetrant system for Puget Sound work

The choice between systems follows the part and the conditions. Water-washable penetrants suit rough castings and large surfaces where a spray rinse is practical, but they need clean water and drainage, which a pier or a vessel deck seldom offers. Solvent-removable systems need only wipes and solvent, so they are the practical choice for a repair on a moored vessel, a terminal structure or a plant. Fluorescent systems work in a shop or a tented, darkened area and detect finer cracks, which matters on critical shafts or on a repair that must stay crack-free for years. Visible dye needs good white light, so overcast Seattle days sometimes call for portable lighting. The procedure names the system, and a Level III approves any change.

How the penetrant process is performed

The method is a fixed sequence. The surface is cleaned and dried, penetrant is applied and left for the dwell the procedure sets, the surplus is removed in the way the procedure specifies, and a developer is applied in a thin even coat. After the development time the surface is examined under white light for visible dye, or in a darkened area under UV-A light for fluorescent penetrant. Solvent-removable visible systems are the usual field choice because they need no water or electricity, while fluorescent systems give more sensitivity where the acceptance class demands it.

Material chemistry matters. On stainless steel and nickel alloys the penetrant materials must be low in sulfur and halogens, and the part is cleaned afterward, because residues can damage those alloys in service. On aluminum the cleaning chemistry must not attack the surface. Each lot of penetrant, remover and developer is recorded, and the technician checks the system with a known reference block or a comparison pass when the procedure calls for it.

Surface preparation and cleaning on marine and shop parts

Most penetrant failures start with the surface. Weld spatter, oxide, paint, oil and salt all keep liquid out of a crack, and ground or machined metal can have smeared over the opening. The procedure therefore names the preparation: brushing or light grinding on welds, solvent cleaning for oil and grease, fresh-water rinsing to remove salt on waterfront parts, and in some cases an etch to reopen smeared metal. The part must be fully dry before penetrant is applied, because water trapped in a crack blocks the penetrant just as paint does.

After the examination the developer and penetrant are removed. On stainless steel and aluminum going back into service, and on any surface that will later be coated or welded, residues are cleaned off and the area is left ready for the next trade. Where a repair is made, the examination is repeated on the finished weld so the file holds the original finding and the clean result side by side.

Common PT findings and how they are reported

A continuous line points to a crack or lap. A line of dots can be a row of pores or a tight crack seen through a rough surface. Scattered round marks usually indicate porosity, and a ragged cluster on a casting suggests shrinkage. On aluminum weld repairs, the usual find is crater cracking and lack of fusion at the toe. On propeller and shaft hardware, fatigue cracks start at keyways, fillets and blade roots. Each indication is described by type, size and location and judged against the criteria in force. Marks that could be false, for example from poor cleaning, are re-examined after recleaning instead of being called defects, so the report distinguishes relevant from non-relevant results. Rejectable indications are marked on the part and sketched, and the owner or surveyor decides how to repair.

Who performs the work

The Atlantis written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, is what qualifies our penetrant technicians. The Level II technician applies the materials, interprets the indications and writes the report; Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, writes or approves the procedure and reviews the report. Atlantis has no office in Seattle. We mobilize crews to your yard, vessel, terminal or plant with the materials and lamps the procedure calls for, and we confirm travel and orientation steps in the quote. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If a class society or customer requires a particular personnel qualification, say so early.

What a PT report contains

The report names the part and location, the procedure and revision, the penetrant, remover and developer by product and lot, the surface and ambient temperature, the dwell and development times, the light level, and the technician and level. Each indication is located and sized with a sketch or photograph, and the result is an accept or reject call against the criteria you named. Where a defect is repaired, the examination is repeated on the repaired area and filed with the original. An ASNT Level III reviews the report before release.

Planning a PT job in Seattle

Temperature and moisture decide most Seattle penetrant jobs. ASME Section V Article 6 covers a part and materials temperature of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, and Puget Sound winter mornings on steel and aluminum often sit near or below the bottom of that range; the crew may need heated enclosures or a procedure qualified for lower temperatures. Rain and wet surfaces stop work until the part is completely dry, because water in a crack keeps penetrant out. Salt on waterfront metal has to be cleaned off first. Dry-dock windows and ferry schedules are fixed, overwater work depends on weather and tides, and refinery and port sites need badge and orientation steps. Tell us about those constraints early and the plan will fit them.

Lighting is a Puget Sound planning item too. Short winter days and overcast skies mean visible-dye examinations often need portable white lighting, and fluorescent work needs a tent or enclosure that can be darkened on a windy pier. The technician measures the light level at the surface and records it, since an examination under poor lighting is not a valid examination. If the part cannot be moved, the enclosure, power and lighting should be part of the scope you send.

PT, MT or UT for your Seattle job

Choose penetrant for non-magnetic metals and machined parts. Choose magnetic particle testing in Seattle for surface cracks in carbon steel. Choose ultrasonic testing in Seattle for remaining wall and internal weld flaws. Our national penetrant testing page describes the service generally, and the MT versus PT comparison helps on mixed-material scopes.

Training your own penetrant technicians

Penetrant is among the easiest methods to bring in house. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, and the penetrant testing training page shows how the course and practical examination fit your written practice. Trainees can practice on the Practical NDT penetrant simulator. For Seattle crews there is a page on NDT training in Seattle, and wider Washington coverage sits on the Washington inspection services page. For written practice work, see written practice development.

faq.q: What can liquid penetrant testing find?
faq.a: Only flaws open to the surface, such as cracks, laps and pores, on non-porous materials. It cannot find a flaw sealed inside the metal, so internal or wall-loss questions need ultrasonic testing instead.

faq.q: Do you have an office in Seattle?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Seattle. Crews are mobilized to your yard, vessel, terminal or plant with the materials and lamps the procedure calls for, and travel and orientation steps are confirmed in the quote.

faq.q: Why choose PT instead of MT on a boat or ferry?
faq.a: Aluminum, stainless steel and bronze are not ferromagnetic, so magnetic particle testing does not work on them. Penetrant works on all of those metals and on carbon steel as well.

faq.q: How does Seattle weather affect penetrant testing?
faq.a: The standard Article 6 range is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, and winter mornings can fall below it. Rain and wet metal also block the penetrant, so we plan heating, enclosures and drying or use a qualified low-temperature procedure.

faq.q: Is penetrant safe on stainless and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Yes, when the materials are the low sulfur and low halogen types the procedure requires and the part is cleaned afterward. We record the product lots in the report so the control can be shown later.

faq.q: Visible dye or fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible dye needs only white light and is the usual field choice. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and is used where the acceptance class requires it, in a darkened area under UV-A light.

faq.q: Which code sets acceptance?
faq.a: The construction or repair code for your item, such as ASME Section VIII Appendix 8, ASME B31.3 or AWS D1.1, or the class or contract rule for a vessel. The owner or surveyor names it before the job.

faq.q: Do penetrant records go to a Washington inspector?
faq.a: For repairs on registered boilers and pressure vessels, yes. The commissioned inspector or owner-user inspection agency reviews the records under the Department of Labor and Industries program and the National Board Inspection Code.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in Seattle, WA: UT and RT Review
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. For Seattle welds, ask about UT or Level III review of radiographs. Request a quote today.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Seattle: What Atlantis Offers Instead
rt.html:
Atlantis does not carry out radiographic testing anywhere in the United States, and that includes Seattle and Puget Sound. If you came here for radiography on a pipeline weld, a shipyard butt weld or a fabricated vessel, this page explains why we do not do it and what we can do: ultrasonic examination where the code and the owner permit it, and independent ASNT Level III review of radiographs made by a licensed contractor. Describe your Seattle scope and we reply within one business day.

Why radiography is not part of our United States services

Industrial radiography uses gamma sources or X-ray equipment, and in the United States it is a licensed activity. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission sets the base rules in 10 CFR Part 34, and Agreement States run their own equivalent programs. Washington is an Agreement State, with radioactive materials licensing handled by the state Department of Health. A company needs a license, certified radiographers, source security and exposure controls before it may expose a weld. Atlantis does not provide that service here. Seattle owners and contractors deserve a clear statement, so that nobody plans a job around a service we cannot lawfully deliver.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric alternative in Seattle

Behind most radiography requests is a simple question: does the weld have flaws inside? Ultrasonic testing answers it without a controlled exclusion area, which is a real advantage on crowded waterfront yards, in occupied refinery units and on terminal structures where clearing an area for exposure stops other trades. Production welds can be examined ultrasonically under provisions in ASME B31.3 and API 1104, groove welds under AWS D1.1 acceptance criteria, and ASME Section VIII Division 1 accepts UT in place of RT only under specific conditions.

The substitution has to be agreed with the owner, the engineer of record and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job and written into the examination plan. Where it is agreed, ultrasonic testing in Seattle from Atlantis covers shear-wave weld examination to a written procedure, with the reference level and indication log in the report. Surface-breaking questions on carbon steel suit magnetic particle testing, and on aluminum or stainless penetrant testing.

ASNT Level III radiograph review, no radiation license needed

Looking at an image uses no source, so it needs no radiation license. A Seattle owner can have an ASNT Level III read radiographs, whether film or digital, alongside their technique sheets, measured against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. The scope can add a second opinion on disputed indications, a check of image quality indicators and film density against the requirement, and a look at an RT contractor's procedure and written practice. The work is directed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Images stay with the contractor who produced them; we review what is sent and report our findings back to you.

It suits Seattle projects where an owner, a general contractor or a surveyor wants an independent opinion on radiography they did not witness, or where an acceptance call is contested. It does not replace the contractor's Level II interpretation. For help setting requirements for a radiography subcontractor, see outsourced Level III consulting.

Radiography training and written practice

If your Seattle team needs to understand radiography, the theory side is covered by the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Hands-on work with sources must still sit inside a licensed program run by the employer. We can also help you write or review the radiography section of an SNT-TC-1A written practice through written practice development. Seattle employers can read about NDT training in Seattle, and statewide inspection services are on the Washington inspection services page.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Seattle?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under NRC rules and Agreement State programs such as the one run in Washington. Ultrasonic testing and radiograph review are available instead.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on my welds?
faq.a: In some cases. Ultrasonic provisions sit in ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1, while Section VIII permits it in place of RT only under stated conditions. Owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree before work.

faq.q: Can you review radiographs made by another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. Film or digital images and technique sheets are read by an ASNT Level III against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, including a second opinion on disputed indications. Images remain with the contractor.

faq.q: Do you recommend a radiography contractor in Seattle?
faq.a: No, radiography contractors are not named or recommended by us. What we can do is read the contractor procedure and the finished images, giving your acceptance decision an independent technical basis.

faq.q: Where can my team learn radiography theory?
faq.a: Theory is covered in the radiographic testing Level 2 course from Atlantis. Source work belongs inside a licensed program, and the employer written practice under SNT-TC-1A decides who is qualified.
